value_chain_position: Multi-country gold/silver producer selling refined dore/concentrate from company-operated mines.
cost_curve_verified: Disagree, and the disagreement matters. The screener's deterministic proxy reads a trailing-twelve-month operating cash margin of 67.8% and files Fortuna in the top cost band; the company's own reported all-in sustaining cost was $2,157 per gold-equivalent ounce in the second quarter of 2026 and $2,107 in the first, both above its published 2026 guidance range of $1,830 to $1,975. The fat margin is a gold-price artifact at $4,443 an ounce, not cost-curve leadership. Only Seguela is genuinely first-quartile at $1,765 all-in and $679 cash cost; Lindero at $2,265 is a fourth-quartile heap leach, and Caylloma's $44.89 per silver-equivalent ounce leaves a thin margin against $65 silver.
gm_trajectory: Gross margin was 57.6% in the second quarter of 2026 on revenue of $318 million, against 61.9% on $342 million in the first quarter and 45.6% on $230 million a year earlier. So margins are up roughly twelve points year over year on a 38% revenue increase, but rolling over sequentially as unit costs rise and gold retreats from its high - revenue fell about 7% quarter on quarter with volumes flat at 72,217 ounces.
bull_thesis:
Fortuna is a debt-free, cash-generating gold producer that has spent the last fifteen months doing the hard, unglamorous things right, and it is priced as though it had not. Start with what is verifiable. It sold its two worst mines - San Jose in Mexico and Yaramoko in Burkina Faso, both within a year of reserve exhaustion - for $84 million of gross proceeds plus a $57.5 million pre-closing dividend, and in doing so removed roughly $50 million of future closure spending. It has since built its balance sheet from a modest net cash position to $614 million of cash and short-term investments against $234 million of total debt (including $95 million of leases) as of 2026-06-30. It bought back $106.6 million of its own stock in the first half of 2026, 10.8 million shares at an average near $9.87, during a drawdown rather than at the peak, shrinking the weighted-average share count from 306.6 million in the first quarter of 2025 to 301.0 million. And it grew proven and probable reserves 50% year over year after depletion, to 3.0 million gold ounces, with indicated resources up 56%. In an industry defined by serial dilution and reserve exhaustion, that combination is genuinely rare.

The operating engine is one excellent mine plus optionality. Seguela in Cote d'Ivoire produced 152,420 ounces in 2025 - above the top of guidance for the second consecutive year - at a cash cost of $679 an ounce and an all-in sustaining cost of $1,560. It has exceeded its mine plan in every quarter of the five on record. On 2026-07-29 the board approved a 30% capacity expansion, taking the plant from 1.75 to 2.3 million tonnes a year for $109 million of construction capital, targeting over 200,000 ounces a year for a decade with a stated 2.5-year payback, funded entirely from operating cash flow.

The second leg is Diamba Sud in Senegal, and its feasibility study published 2026-06-29 is the strongest single document in this file: a 60% after-tax internal rate of return and a $1.0 billion net present value at a 5% discount rate, using $3,500 gold - well below today's $4,443 - on $398 million of initial capital, over a 9.4-year life producing 1.05 million ounces, averaging 158,000 ounces a year in the first four years at an all-in sustaining cost of $1,056. The environmental decree arrived 2026-06-15 and the supporting technical report was filed 2026-07-13. Management said in the first quarter of 2025 that it would have a construction decision in the second half of 2026 and it has hit every intermediate gate. If built as designed, Diamba would be the company's lowest-cost mine and would pull the consolidated cost position - the single biggest thing wrong with this company - down toward the industry middle.

Put those together and the 2028 shape is roughly 500,000 ounces a year at a blended all-in sustaining cost near $1,600, against roughly 290,000 ounces at $2,100 today, with no equity issuance and no project debt required. At a $3,800 gold deck that is on the order of $770 million of after-tax operating cash a year on about 327 million fully diluted shares.

The valuation supports the case even before that arrives. Fortuna trades at about 3.55 times enterprise value to trailing operating cash profitability, against 3.64 for B2Gold, 7.01 for SSR Mining, 7.77 for Alamos, 9.45 for Pan American Silver and 11.61 for Coeur - the cheapest in its own competitive set. Its free-cash-flow yield of about 12.8% is roughly double the next best and five times what Alamos or B2Gold offer. Conditions the case depends on: gold holding above roughly $3,500; Diamba being built within 15% of its $398 million budget; Cote d'Ivoire and Senegal keeping their fiscal terms; and consolidated costs bending back toward guidance in the second half of 2026 as management has promised.
bear_thesis:
The bear case is not that Fortuna is a bad company. It is that the market is being asked to pay a normal price for an above-average operating story whose earnings are, right now, almost entirely a function of a metal price that has already run and already begun to correct - and that the moment to buy it passed about three weeks ago.

Start with the price action, because it is the whole timing argument. On 2026-07-30 Fortuna traded at $8.37. Today it is $10.755, up about 26% in a month and 15% in five days, on the back of three pieces of news that have now all happened: the Diamba feasibility study (2026-06-29), the Seguela expansion approval (2026-07-29) and the second-quarter result (2026-08-05). The re-rating those events were supposed to force has already been paid for. Anyone underwriting the stock today is underwriting it after the news, not before.

Now the operating reality behind the multiple. Fortuna is a high-cost producer wearing a high-margin costume. Consolidated all-in sustaining cost was $2,157 an ounce in the second quarter of 2026 and $2,107 in the first - both above the company's own 2026 guidance range of $1,830 to $1,975, for two consecutive quarters. Management attributes about $49 an ounce to outside forces and $115 to one-time items; strip both and you still get roughly $1,993, above the top of the range. A cost guide missed twice in the first half is a guide, not a fact. And the composition is uncomfortable: Lindero in Argentina runs at $2,265 an ounce, suffered two mechanical failures in the fourth quarter of 2025 that put full-year production about 6% below the bottom of guidance, then required a 35-day shutdown in March 2026 after an engineering review found structural fatigue in the primary crusher foundations. Caylloma's $44.89 per silver-equivalent ounce leaves roughly $20 of margin against $65 silver - a metal that has fallen from $121 to $65 in a year.

The torque cuts both ways and it is large. A 10% move in gold swings operating cash profitability by about 14%, and the stock's two-year sensitivity to the gold price is 1.67 times. Gold is $4,443 today against a 200-day average of $4,587 and a 52-week high of $5,626 - it is already 21% off its peak and below its own trend. Silver is 46% off its high. If gold retraces to $3,000 - below the $3,353 52-week low, but not an outlandish number after a run of this size - trailing operating cash profitability falls from roughly $820 million toward $450 million. Lindero at $3,000 gold earns roughly $950 an ounce before tax and becomes a candidate for a shortened mine plan, not an expansion. Caylloma at proportionally weaker silver is close to break-even. And Diamba Sud, whose 60% return was struck at $3,500, becomes a project you defer rather than a project you rush - which is precisely when a $398 million capital commitment becomes dangerous rather than accretive.

That is the specific risk in the next two years: this company has committed to spend roughly $330 million in 2026, $398 million on Diamba and $109 million on the Seguela expansion, plus $25 million more for owner-operated Sunbird underground development. The $435 million of net cash the bulls point to is not a war chest sitting idle; it is the funding for that programme. Net cash already fell from $456 million at 2026-03-31 to $372 million at 2026-06-30 - a drop of $84 million in a single quarter, with capital spending rising from $45 million to $68 million and buybacks of $82 million. In a weaker gold tape the buyback stops first, then the exploration budget, then the growth timetable.

There is also a quieter governance point. The company sold $172.5 million of 3.75% convertible notes in June 2024 at a $6.59 conversion price. Those are now well in the money - roughly 26 million shares, the gap between the 301.0 million basic and 328.6 million diluted counts. So the $106.6 million of buybacks at about $9.87 is partly repurchasing an exposure the company sold at $6.59. Per-share arithmetic should use 327 million shares, not 301 million, and doing so takes roughly 8% off every per-share figure the bull case quotes.

Finally, the discount is not free money. Fortuna trades at 3.55 times trailing operating cash profitability against a peer median near 7.8 for a reason: Argentina, Peru, Cote d'Ivoire, Senegal, and now Guyana and Suriname; a consolidated cost position in the industry's expensive half; and a reserve life near ten years against fifteen to twenty at Alamos or Pan American. A ten-year mine discounted at 8% is worth roughly five times operating cash profitability, not eight. Much of the apparent cheapness is the correct price of a shorter, riskier asset base. What would confirm the bear: a third consecutive quarter of all-in sustaining cost above $2,000, a Diamba capital estimate revised above $450 million, any change in Senegalese or Ivorian mining fiscal terms, or gold closing below $3,800.
sop_bull:

Per-share figures use 327 million fully diluted shares, treating the June 2024 convertible notes as converted (which also extinguishes their $139 million of debt).

- Seguela, Cote d'Ivoire: 170,000 ounces a year through 2028 rising to 200,000 after the approved expansion, at an all-in sustaining cost near $1,750-$1,800, taxed at 25%, discounted at 8% over ten years and net of the $109 million expansion capital, then reduced to the 90% attributable interest. Value $2,186 million, or $6.68 a share.
- Lindero, Argentina: 97,000 ounces at $2,265 all-in, taxed at 35%, discounted at 12% for country risk over eight years. Value $681 million, or $2.08 a share.
- Caylloma, Peru: a small silver-lead-zinc mine earning roughly $20 an ounce of silver-equivalent margin on 2.5 million ounces. Value $250 million, or $0.76 a share.
- Diamba Sud, Senegal: the June 2026 feasibility study's $1.0 billion net present value at $3,500 gold, marked up for spot and taken at 0.7 times to reflect that it is unbuilt. Value $1,050 million, or $3.21 a share.
- Exploration and reserve-life extension beyond the ten-year window - Sunbird Deep, Kingfisher, Tongon North, Diamba's open mineralisation, Guyana: $700 million, or $2.14 a share.
- Net cash: $614 million of cash and short-term investments less $95 million of lease obligations, with the convertible notes converted rather than repaid. $519 million, or $1.59 a share.
- Equity investments including the 15% stake in Awale Resources: $50 million, or $0.15 a share.
- Less capitalised corporate overhead of roughly $29 million a year: minus $180 million, or minus $0.55 a share.

sop_bear:
Adverse sum-of-the-parts, assuming the precious-metals cycle turns against it: gold falls to $3,000 an ounce - a 32% decline from today, below the $3,353 52-week low - and silver falls proportionally. This is the scenario the symmetric torque describes: a 10% gold move swings operating cash profitability about 14%, so a 32% move takes trailing operating cash profitability from roughly $820 million to roughly $450 million.

- Seguela: still the good mine, earning roughly $1,500 an ounce of margin as price-linked royalties fall with the metal, but discounted harder and with the expansion's economics thinner. Value $1,150 million, or $3.52 a share.
- Lindero: margin collapses to roughly $950 an ounce before tax on 97,000 ounces, about $60 million after tax. At that level the mine plan shortens rather than extends; valued over six years at a 12% discount. Value $220 million, or $0.67 a share.
- Caylloma: close to break-even on weaker silver. Value $80 million, or $0.24 a share.
- Diamba Sud: the feasibility study's 60% return was struck at $3,500 gold; at $3,000 the project is deferred rather than accelerated, and an unbuilt project needing $398 million of capital in a bear tape is marked near option value. Value $150 million, or $0.46 a share.
- Exploration and reserve extension: written to zero - in a bear tape exploration budgets are the first line cut.
- Net cash: holds near $450 million rather than compounding, because operating cash roughly matches the committed capital programme. $1.38 a share.
- Equity investments: written to zero.
- Less capitalised corporate overhead: minus $180 million, or minus $0.55 a share.

Total $1,870 million, or about $5.72 a share. A cross-check from the other direction gives a similar answer: the stock's two-year sensitivity to gold is 1.67 times, so a 32% decline in the metal implies roughly a 53% decline in the equity, or about $5.06. sop_breakdown:
Base case, using a $3,800 gold deck - 14% below today's $4,443 spot, above the $3,500 the company used in its own Diamba feasibility study, and a deliberate refusal to underwrite a metal that has already run 21% off its high forever. Per-share figures use 327 million fully diluted shares.

- Seguela, Cote d'Ivoire (the flagship, including the approved 30% expansion and Sunbird underground): $1,730 million, $5.29 a share. This is 44% of the total and the reason to own the company at all.
- Diamba Sud, Senegal, at 0.6 times the feasibility study's $1.0 billion net present value to reflect that it is permitted and funded but not yet built: $650 million, $1.99 a share.
- Exploration and reserve-life extension beyond ten years: $530 million, $1.62 a share. Justified by reserves growing 50% year over year after depletion, not by hope.
- Net cash after leases, with the convertible notes treated as converted: $519 million, $1.59 a share.
- Lindero, Argentina: $500 million, $1.53 a share - a high-cost, mechanically unreliable heap leach worth roughly one-third of Seguela despite producing more than half its ounces.
- Caylloma, Peru: $150 million, $0.46 a share.
- Equity investments including Awale Resources: $25 million, $0.08 a share.
- Less capitalised corporate overhead: minus $180 million, minus $0.55 a share.

Total $3,924 million, or $12.00 a share. Two cross-checks bracket it. A multiple approach - roughly $655 million of operating cash profitability at $3,800 gold on a fair 5 times, which is what a ten-year reserve life supports, plus net cash and risked Diamba - gives about $13.60. The 2028 steady state of 500,000 ounces at a blended $1,600 all-in cost, discounted back two and a half years at 10%, gives $11 to $15 depending on the exit multiple. Twelve dollars sits honestly in the middle.
risk_reward: From $10.755 today: the adverse case sits at $5.60, the base case at $12.00, the favorable case at $15.50. The distance down to the adverse case is more than four times the distance up to the base case. That asymmetry is the entire timing argument - three weeks ago, at $8.37, the same three numbers described a genuinely attractive setup; today they do not. There is no structural floor beneath the equity: net cash is $1.59 a share fully diluted, there is no deal, no tender and no dividend, and an active buyback is a support, not a floor.
catalyst_status_note: Every load-bearing event has already happened and the stock has already paid for them. The Senegalese environmental decree for Diamba Sud arrived 2026-06-15; the feasibility study, showing a 60% after-tax internal rate of return and a $1.0 billion net present value at $3,500 gold on $398 million of capital, was published 2026-06-29; the supporting technical report was filed 2026-07-13; the board approved a 30% capacity expansion at Seguela on 2026-07-29; second-quarter results were reported 2026-08-05. Fortuna traded at $8.37 on 2026-07-30 and $10.755 today - up about 26% in a month and 15% in the last five days. Under this lane's rules a spent catalyst is neither a plus nor a penalty for a clean-forensic franchise, so this status does not drive the verdict; the verdict is driven by what is left between the price and fair value after that move. The next dated event is the third-quarter report, expected early November 2026.
peer_comps_note:
Against the assigned competitive set, Fortuna is the cheapest name on every cash-based measure and the reason is only half unfair. On enterprise value to trailing operating cash profitability: Fortuna 3.55 times, B2Gold 3.64, SSR Mining 7.01, Alamos Gold 7.77, Pan American Silver 9.45, Coeur Mining 11.61 - a peer median near 7.8. On free-cash-flow yield Fortuna prints about 12.8% against SSR Mining 7.9%, Pan American 6.3%, Coeur 6.1%, B2Gold 2.5% and Alamos 2.3%. Returns are competitive too: return on invested capital of about 18.8% against Alamos at 14.8% and Pan American at 12.5%.

But the discount is not pure mispricing. Fortuna's company reserve life is about ten years against fifteen to twenty at Alamos and Pan American, its consolidated all-in sustaining cost of $2,157 an ounce sits in the industry's expensive half, and its asset base spans Argentina, Peru, Cote d'Ivoire and Senegal. A ten-year mine discounted at 8% is arithmetically worth roughly five times operating cash profitability, not eight - so the honest gap is 3.55 times against a fair 5.0 to 5.5, not against the 7.8 peer median. Fortuna's closest true analogue is B2Gold, which trades at the same multiple for the same reason: excellent assets in jurisdictions the market refuses to pay full price for.
consensus_delta:
There are two places where the market is looking the wrong way, and they point in opposite directions - which is why this resolves to waiting rather than buying.

Where the market is too pessimistic: it prices Fortuna at 3.55 times trailing operating cash profitability against a peer median near 7.8, as though the asset base were static and the balance sheet leveraged. Neither is true. Reserves grew 50% year over year after depletion to 3.0 million gold ounces, indicated resources 56%, and Sunbird's reserves 34%. The company holds $614 million of cash against $234 million of debt and is funding a growth programme that takes production from roughly 290,000 to over 500,000 ounces entirely from its own cash flow - no equity, no streaming deal, no project finance. Coverage is genuinely thin: only one price target printed in the last quarter, and the question queues on several of these calls emptied early with private investors filling the gap. Thin coverage is where mispricing lives.

Where the market is too optimistic, and this is the part that governs today's decision: the sell-side anchor is a $14.50 target set on 2026-07-30 when the stock was $8.37. That target is now only 35% above a price that has already moved 26% in a month. The street has not raised it since; it has simply been overtaken. More substantively, consensus appears to be carrying the company's own 2026 all-in sustaining cost guidance of $1,830 to $1,975 an ounce as a fact. It is not. Reported costs were $2,107 in the first quarter and $2,157 in the second, and even stripping management's own $49 of external and $115 of one-time explanations leaves roughly $1,993 - above the top of the range. Two consecutive quarters above a guide is a pattern, and the second-half improvement management promises has been promised in similar language before.

The third, quieter error is arithmetical. Per-share figures quoted from the 301 million basic share count overstate value by about 8%. The June 2024 convertible notes, struck at a $6.59 conversion price, are well in the money and represent roughly 26 million shares; the diluted count is 328.6 million. Any model running $10 of value on 301 million shares is running $9.20 on the honest count.
valley_of_death:
The next three to nine months contain no crisis, but they do contain three specific ways this gets cheaper before it gets dearer.

First, the cost guide gets formally missed. Consolidated all-in sustaining cost has printed $2,107 and $2,157 against a $1,830-$1,975 annual range. Management says unit costs within its control will trend back inside the range in the second half. If the third-quarter report in early November shows a third consecutive quarter above $2,000, the market will stop treating the overrun as timing and start treating it as the cost base - and a company whose whole equity story is 'we are cheap on cash flow' cannot afford to have the cash flow re-based.

Second, the cash pile visibly stops growing. It already has: net cash fell from $456 million at 2026-03-31 to $372 million at 2026-06-30, an $84 million drawdown in one quarter, as capital spending rose from $45 million to $68 million and $82 million went to buybacks. The committed programme is roughly $330 million of capital in 2026, $398 million for Diamba Sud, $109 million for the Seguela expansion and $25 million more for owner-operated Sunbird development. Investors who bought a cash-rich producer in the first half of 2026 will spend the second half watching that cash convert into construction in Senegal, and construction in Senegal does not look like a balance sheet - it looks like a risk.

Third, and most powerful, the metal. Gold at $4,443 sits below its own 200-day average of $4,587 and 21% below its 52-week high of $5,626; silver has fallen from $121 to $65. The precious-metals complex is in a correction, and Fortuna has decoupled upward from it over the past month on company news. Company news has a shelf life; the metal does not. A 10% decline in gold takes roughly 14% out of operating cash profitability, and the equity's two-year sensitivity to the metal is 1.67 times. A move to $4,000 gold - unremarkable inside this correction - plausibly returns the stock to $9 without a single thing going wrong operationally.

One genuine operational hazard sits alongside these: Lindero. It broke twice in the fourth quarter of 2025, put full-year production 6% below the bottom of guidance, and required a 35-day shutdown in March 2026 after structural fatigue was found in the crusher foundations. It is also the highest-cost mine at $2,265 an ounce. Another failure there is a live possibility, not a tail risk.
positioning_washout:
The forced-selling dynamics here are unusual and worth understanding, because they cut in both directions.

The legacy holder base was assembled for a company that no longer exists. Fortuna Silver Mines became Fortuna Mining, and gold dore is now effectively all of revenue - $820 million of $824 million in the 2025 segment disclosure. The ticker still reads FSM. Silver-focused funds and silver-focused retail investors own a business that is 95% a gold producer, and the calls make that base audible: a private investor on the first-quarter 2025 call saying he had been 'buying all the way down,' a newsletter writer arranging a podcast appearance on air. This is a retail-and-newsletter-heavy register, which means the holder base is momentum-sensitive rather than valuation-anchored, and it means a metal drawdown produces selling that has nothing to do with the mines.

That is the real washout risk: silver is 46% off its high. If silver-linked funds see redemptions, they sell what is in the sleeve, and Fortuna is still in silver sleeves for historical reasons.

There is no dividend, so there is no yield-focused base to lose - the company pays nothing and has said buybacks are its preferred method of returning capital. And there is a genuine counterweight: the company itself is the marginal buyer. It repurchased $82 million of stock in the second quarter of 2026 alone and $106.6 million in the first half, 10.8 million shares, at an average near $9.87. That is real support, and notably it was bid during the drawdown rather than at the top. But it is support, not a floor - a buyback is discretionary, it is the first thing cut in a weak tape, and it is competing for the same dollars as $398 million of Diamba construction. Do not mistake it for structural protection.
forcing_function:
There is no single dated event that forces a re-rating from here, because the events that were going to force one have already fired. The environmental decree (2026-06-15), the Diamba Sud feasibility study (2026-06-29), the technical report filing (2026-07-13), the Seguela expansion approval (2026-07-29) and the second-quarter result (2026-08-05) all landed inside eight weeks, and the stock moved from $8.37 to $10.755 in response. That re-rating has been paid for.

What remains is a sequence of verification points rather than catalysts:

- Third-quarter 2026 results, expected early November 2026. This is the real test, and it is a cost test, not a production test. Consolidated all-in sustaining cost below $2,000 an ounce would validate management's second-half promise and re-open the case; a third quarter above $2,000 breaks the cost guide and, with it, the argument that the trailing cash-flow multiple is a fair basis for valuation.
- The formal construction decision and first concrete at Diamba Sud, expected in the second half of 2026 following the exploitation permit. Watch the capital number, not the ceremony: $398 million holding is a green light, anything materially above $450 million converts the growth story into a capital-discipline story.
- Fourth-quarter 2025-style reserve and resource update, historically published in February and April. Reserve replacement is what justifies extending the ten-year mine life that carries roughly $1.62 a share of my base case.
- Sunbird underground permitting in Cote d'Ivoire, targeted for completion during 2026, with initial development in 2027 and first ore in 2028.

The honest answer for a director is that the forcing function for this name has become the gold price plus a cost proof-point, and neither is a date you can underwrite.
moderator_conclusion:
This is a good company at a price that is no longer generous, and the discipline is to say so rather than to reach.

What is genuinely true about Fortuna: management has done the hard things and can be checked on all of them. It sold its two worst mines near reserve exhaustion. It grew reserves 50% year over year after depletion. It repurchased $106.6 million of stock during a drawdown while the share count fell rather than rose - which, in a sector whose besetting sin is serial dilution, is the strongest single signal in the file. It delivered the Seguela mine above the top of guidance for two consecutive years at a cash cost of $679 an ounce. And it has published a feasibility study for Diamba Sud showing a 60% after-tax return and a $1.0 billion net present value at a gold price well below spot, on capital it can fund from its own cash flow. There is no financing kill-switch here, no serial dilution, no capacity inflation, and no promoter's balance sheet. The one presentational lapse - aggregating 3.0 million ounces of reserves with 2.2 million ounces of the least certain resource category into 'over 7 million ounces' - was flagged by the chief executive himself as he did it.

What is also true, and decides this: Fortuna is not a low-cost producer, it is a high-margin producer because gold is $4,443. Consolidated all-in sustaining cost of $2,157 an ounce is above the company's own 2026 guidance for the second consecutive quarter, and the composition is one excellent mine (Seguela at $1,765), one marginal and mechanically unreliable one (Lindero at $2,265, in Argentina), and a small silver mine earning about $20 an ounce. The proxy metrics in this file read a 67.8% margin and file the company in the top cost band; that reading is an artifact of the metal price and I am recording the disagreement explicitly.

The torque is symmetric and it is the dominant variable for at least two more years, until Diamba pours. A 10% move in gold swings operating cash profitability about 14%, and the equity's sensitivity to the metal is 1.67 times. Gold is already 21% below its 52-week high and below its 200-day average; silver is 46% below. Against that backdrop Fortuna has risen 26% in a month on company-specific news that has now all been published.

So the arithmetic. My base sum-of-the-parts, at a $3,800 gold deck and on 327 million fully diluted shares, is $12.00 - carried mostly by Seguela at $5.29 and Diamba at $1.99, with $1.59 of net cash. The favorable case, if gold simply holds today's level, is $15.50. The adverse case, if the cycle turns and gold reaches $3,000, is $5.60, cross-checked against the beta-implied $5.06. From $10.755 the distance down is more than four times the distance up to fair value. Three weeks ago at $8.37 those same three numbers described a compelling seat. Today they describe a stock that has done most of its work.

The verdict is to wait, and I will name the level rather than gesture at a flush: I want Fortuna back at $8.75 or below - which restores a meaningful discount to the $12.00 base case and roughly the setup that existed before the July-August news cycle - or, alternatively, a third-quarter report in early November showing consolidated all-in sustaining cost below $2,000 an ounce, which would validate the cost guide, lift the base case, and justify paying up. Either one is a buy trigger. Neither is available today. The value case is real, the forensics are clean, and the discount is no longer large enough to pay for the metal risk sitting underneath it.
